Self-evolving Agent Harness

Chuyang Wei Affiliation: Zhongguancun Academy Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Haoxiang Guan Affiliation: Zhongguancun Academy Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Minghang Zhu Affiliation: Zhongguancun Academy    Kexin Zhou Affiliation: Zhongguancun Academy Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Jiyan He Affiliation: Zhongguancun Academy Affiliation: Zhongguancun Institute of Artificial Intelligence    Xiren Zhou Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Huanhuan Chen Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Yifei Shen Affiliation: Zhongguancun Academy Affiliation: Zhongguancun Institute of Artificial Intelligence Affiliation: Corresponding author
Abstract

Harness self-evolution revises an agent’s software scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while keeping model weights fixed. We formalize a feedback-driven process in which accepted revisions persist across runs. The framework separates update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms. It distinguishes changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. We characterize search through evolutionary optimization and examine its reliability through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions, the analysis yields an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule using fresh, independent validation data. We examine how persistent harness revisions affect knowledge sharing and organizational workflows, with implications for scientific reliability, physical safety, and institutional accountability. Cases from prior work illustrate model–harness co-design, distributed execution, and plugin reuse. Reliable deployment requires continual validation as task distributions and evaluators change, with independent safeguards for learning, runtime privileges, and consequential actions. We provide a comprehensive 66-page discussion of related work, theory, algorithms, evaluation, applications, and the broader impact of Harness RSI, together with continuously updated code and supplementary materials, at https://github.com/zgcagi/Harness-RSI.

1 Introduction

As tasks and environments change after deployment, agents need mechanisms for continued adaptation. Harness self-evolution uses execution feedback to revise instructions, memory, and control logic while keeping model weights fixed. Later runs load accepted revisions, and the update mechanism remains available to learn from subsequent experience (Section 2). This process builds on recursive self-improvement and self-referential problem solving in the context of contemporary agents (good1965ultraintelligent; schmidhuber2003godel).

Adaptation can revise model weights or the harness governing prompts, memory, workflows, and tools. Our focus on the latter rests on three considerations. First, the harness directly shapes a fixed model’s behavior, while reusable procedures preserve task constraints and lessons from earlier failures (chan2025mlebench; zhao2024expel; wang2024voyager). Second, harness revisions reuse an existing model deployment, avoiding retraining and additional weight checkpoints. This can reduce adaptation and maintenance costs and permits updates through proprietary APIs without access to model weights. Third, instructions, memory records, and code support direct inspection, version comparison, and change tracking; attributing behavioral differences between model checkpoints can require additional controlled experiments. We hold the task model fixed to isolate harness self-evolution, with joint model–harness evolution addressed in Section .

Existing methods vary in what is modified, how candidates are generated, and how revisions are admitted (shinn2023reflexion; zhao2024expel; wang2024voyager; zhang2025aflow; robeyns2025selfimproving). We first classify the update target: the state modified and inherited by later runs. Interpreted-state updates revise instructions, stored experience, or task-level coordination over predefined capabilities; executable revisions change capability implementations, runtime control logic, or plugin-based service composition (Section 3; Figure 1). Empirical selection alone does not establish generalization or retention. Section  relates candidate search to evolutionary structures, then uses stability and concentration results to state conditions for expected generalization, bounded accumulated regressions, and high-probability admission. Persistent state also determines how revisions propagate and which consequences software recovery can address, motivating system design choices, continual validation, and independent safety controls (Sections –).

This work makes three contributions:

  • •

    Definition and Operational Taxonomy (Sections 2–3). We define a persistent feedback-driven lifecycle and organize interpreted-state updates and executable revisions by their mutation boundaries.

  • •

    Conditional Theoretical Analysis (Section ). We map harness search to evolutionary structures and derive conditions for expected generalization, bounded accumulated regressions, and high-probability admission from classical stability and concentration results.

  • •

    Systems Implications and Design Trade-offs (Sections –). We analyze propagation and repair burdens in five settings and connect attributed cases (Sections 3 and ) to model–harness pairing, deployment, and reuse decisions, with continual validation and safety constraints.

Associated resources are available at https://github.com/zgcagi/Harness-RSI.

2 Definition of Harness Self-Evolution

Harness.

Following the model–harness decomposition (deepseek2026harness), we define a harness HH as the software and configuration governing a model MM’s execution in a task environment EE. Table 1 summarizes seven runtime functions. Model adapters are part of HH; learned parameters are part of MM. Execution produces a rollout, which is scored by JJ:

τ∼Run⁡(M,H,E),y=J⁡(τ).\tau\sim\operatorname{Run}(M,H,E),\qquad y=J(\tau). (1)

The final assessment JJ includes scoring, outcome verification, and the records that determine the result. Candidates may revise internal critics or provisional checks within HH, but cannot modify JJ.

Harness self-evolution.

Harness self-evolution uses execution experience to iteratively revise HH, aiming to improve task performance or resource efficiency while holding MM fixed. At round k≥1k\geq 1, the incumbent Hk−1H_{k-1} generates a batch of bb rollouts, each including its trajectory, outcome, and available feedback:

ℬk\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{k} ={τk,i}i=1b,τk,i∼Run⁡(M,Hk−1,Ek,i),\displaystyle=\{\tau_{k,i}\}_{i=1}^{b},\qquad\tau_{k,i}\sim\operatorname{Run}(M,H_{k-1},E_{k,i}), (2)
Hk\displaystyle H_{k} =Update⁡(Hk−1,ℬk).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Update}(H_{k-1},\mathcal{B}_{k}). (3)

The update operator combines diagnosis, proposal, assessment, and admission. It may draw on historical feedback, archived candidates, and additional validation rollouts. If no revision is admitted, the incumbent is retained: Hk=Hk−1H_{k}=H_{k-1}.

Each retained revision changes the state used for subsequent execution, whose feedback can guide the next update. This lifecycle requires:

  1. 1.

    Operational feedback and update continuity. The system uses feedback from its own executions to construct or select revisions algorithmically, and retains the mechanism for further updates. Environments, automated assessors, and people may provide feedback; admission may require human approval.

  2. 2.

    Persistence across runs. Accepted revisions are stored and loaded in a subsequent run, allowing experience from one interaction to influence later execution.

These requirements concern repeatability: one observed update can demonstrate the capability if both hold. Appending logs or compacting context under fixed rules does not revise the harness; learning reusable procedures or changing memory policies can. Revising the update mechanism adds another level of recursion.

Scope and terminology.

Self-evolution denotes the update process; self-improvement denotes a gain established by comparison. We use harness RSI (recursive self-improvement) as the name of the research area, without assuming that each revision helps. Weight-only adaptation and scaffolds without an update mechanism fall outside this scope. When a system also trains weights, we examine its harness updates with the task model held fixed.

3 The Taxonomy of Harness Self-Evolution

EURISKO’s heuristic revision and the Gödel Machine’s proof-governed self-rewriting established distinct antecedents of harness self-evolution (lenat1983eurisko; schmidhuber2003godel). Contemporary methods use empirical feedback to revise prompts, consolidate persistent memory, and search workflow specifications around a fixed model (agrawal2026gepa; fernando2024promptbreeder; zhao2024expel; wang2025workflow; zhang2025aflow). The interpreted/executable distinction concerns the edited artifact’s role, not its programming language. Workflow revisions remain interpreted when they change task-level sequencing or routing through fixed coordination interfaces over predefined operators. This includes code that only composes those operators; revising operator implementations or the runtime mechanisms that enact coordination constitutes an executable revision, even under an unchanged executor.

We organize executable targets into component implementations, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. The first two describe mutation scope; the third describes how components and runtime services are bound and replaced. Plugin composition can span component implementations and repository-level logic, so a revision may belong to more than one category. Classifying the update target does not determine whether a method satisfies the feedback, continuity, and persistence requirements in Section 2.

3.1 Tools and Code Patches

Component-level revision confines mutation to callable procedures or designated modules while keeping surrounding orchestration outside the editable surface. Where entry points and I/O contracts remain fixed, candidates replace component implementations; tool synthesis may instead extend the callable interface. Skill libraries retain executable functions for later retrieval and composition (wang2024voyager; yu2025polyskill); patch-based architectures, including Self-Harness, HarnessCompass, and Agentic Harness Engineering, constrain trace-guided mutation to selected components (zhang2026selfharness; zhang2026harnesscompass; lin2026agentic). Editing memory-management functions changes the harness machinery, whereas curating stored entries changes its interpreted state (zhang2025memevolve). Within this boundary, candidate archives preserve alternatives for subsequent search (luo2026harnessbank), while protocol perturbations test whether an evolved harness’s gain over the initial harness survives changes in assessment conditions (zhu2026badgenius). Stable interfaces facilitate replacement and local checks, but changed outputs or shared state can propagate regressions beyond the edited module.

3.2 Repository and Runtime Logic

Repository-level search exposes context construction, orchestration loops, execution hooks, recovery, and termination to revision. The boundary concerns control over interactions among harness components, rather than the number of files edited. Whole-agent synthesis searches complete control programs, while repository evolution retains implementation lineages for later selection and revision (hu2025automated; lee2026metaharness; robeyns2025selfimproving; zhang2026darwin; zhang2026darwinx; wang2025huxley). Changes to shared context, scheduling, or recovery can alter the inputs and execution assumptions of otherwise unchanged components. This coupling motivates edit constraints, transfer-oriented admission, and deployment checks (xia2026rrsi; cai2026moss). Archive membership preserves a candidate for further search; adoption additionally requires promoting the selected program into the runtime used by later tasks. Extending mutation to the optimizer’s prompts, hooks, and tools makes the update mechanism itself evolvable (wang2026verse). An exported program satisfies the continuing lifecycle only if its deployment retains an update mechanism.

HarnessOpt extends the SkillOpt-Lite study from skill editing to runtime revision, improving spreadsheet previews, output checks, and recovery after tool failures (shen2026skilloptlite). On SpreadsheetBench (Table 2), GPT-5.4-nano with HarnessOpt and skill reaches 77.58%, exceeding GPT-5.5 with SkillOpt (76.20%); across all four models, HarnessOpt with skill improves on SkillOpt-Lite by 5.69–11.39 percentage points. This crossover illustrates model–harness pairing, but does not establish superiority at matched cost.

3.3 Everything Is a Plugin

Plugin architectures organize mutation through declared interfaces, dependency constraints, and lifecycle operations. The editable object may be a component implementation or a binding that determines which implementation supplies a runtime service, such as memory storage, tool dispatch, or the agent loop. Composition here therefore reaches beyond task-level routing among fixed operators. Kernel-defined substrates specify how these services are connected, mounted, and replaced (deepseek2026harness; shi2026programming); feedback-driven systems revise typed primitives, versioned resources, or scoped modules under interface and validation constraints (chen2026harnessx; li2026argus; zhang2026autogenesis; wu2026modularrsi). This organization can expose both local capabilities and core runtime services while retaining explicit constraints on their composition. Everything Is a Plugin (EIP) extends it to capabilities generated, validated, and mounted during operation. Interface contracts support compatibility checks and component replacement; they do not establish behavioral isolation or safe admission. Adoption still requires validation of the composed behavior.

Using DSH Everything, a Codex plugin lets the agent generate tools during execution and retain them for later tasks (shen2026dsheverything; pan2026eip). In a simulated office workload, spreadsheets from different company regions vary in language and content but share similar calculations. Codex creates batch-lookup and summarization tools: first-task tool calls fall from 13 to 3, while wall time rises by 54.9% and tokens by 15.7%. A separately reported cumulative series shows savings from the second task, reaching 110,351 tokens and 22.97 s after five tasks (Table 3). The first-task totals imply increases of 6,453 tokens and 8.51 s, whereas cumulative row 1 reports 4,895 tokens and 6.74 s. This unresolved difference prevents treating the two reports as a single cost trajectory; negative cumulative differences indicate savings.
